items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why conflicts arise in the management of degraded environments. (b) Explain why involving local stakeholders can improve environmental management.
items.answer: (a) Stakeholders have different priorities (profit, jobs, health, conservation); costs and benefits fall on different groups; uncertainty over causes; who pays; short-term vs long-term interests. (b) Local knowledge; greater acceptance and compliance; fairer sharing of benefits; long-term commitment and monitoring.

items.stem: Researchers measured the height and annual migration distance of 8 barchan dunes in the Kharga depression, Egypt. Table 2.3 gives, for each dune, the dune height (m) and the migration distance (m per year). Dune 1: 8.6, 60. Dune 2: 11.2, 52. Dune 3: 14.1, 43. Dune 4: 14.4, 30. Dune 5: 14.5, 47. Dune 6: 17.2, 32. Dune 7: 17.4, 22. Dune 8: 22, 3. Critical values of rs for n = 8: 0.643 (0.05 level) and 0.833 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: Wind speed and sand supply may differ between dunes; measure over several years and choose dunes in one dune field.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why Japan is a hazardous environment. (b) Explain why management did not prevent large losses in the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami.
items.answer: (a) It lies where four plates meet (Pacific, Philippine Sea, Eurasian, North American): earthquakes, tsunamis and over 100 active volcanoes; typhoons, heavy rain and landslides; dense coastal population. (b) The tsunami (up to about 40 m locally) overtopped walls designed for smaller events; people relied on walls and earlier warnings underestimated the height; the Fukushima nuclear accident added a technological disaster.

items.stem: Fig. 10.3 shows the cumulative displacement (mm) recorded by an extensometer on a slope above a road in Hong Kong: day 0: 0, day 7: 3.5, day 14: 7.7, day 21: 14.7, day 28: 23.1, day 35: 32.2. Engineers issue an alert when the rate of movement exceeds 1.5 mm per day. (a) Identify the periods in which an alert should have been issued. (b) Explain why an increasing rate of movement is a warning sign.
items.answer: (a) None: the rate never exceeded the threshold. (b) Acceleration shows that shear strength is falling relative to stress, often as water pressure rises or a slip surface develops, and may precede rapid failure.

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $45, Mexico $4, China $7, Vietnam $3, Bangladesh $1. Assembling a shirt takes 0.8 hours of labour. A TNC plans to make 2 000 000 units a year. Calculate the labour cost per unit in each country.
items.answer: the USA: $36; Mexico: $3.2; China: $5.6; Vietnam: $2.4; Bangladesh: $0.8

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Sea level rise is the same everywhere on Earth.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Sub-aerial processes are unimportant where waves are powerful.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Relative sea-level change varies with land movement, ocean currents and gravity effects. (b) Not correct. Waves remove debris, but weathering and mass movement still supply much of the material and shape cliff profiles.

items.stem: Country P, an emerging economy, had GDP per capita (constant US$) of 800 in 2000 and 2 590 in 2025. Use the rule of 70 to estimate how long it took GDP per capita to double.
items.answer: about 14.5 years

items.stem: A government gave a foreign car-parts company US$90 million in grants and tax relief to open a factory in an enterprise zone in north-east England. The factory employs 800 people at an average wage of US$34 000 a year. The regional employment multiplier is estimated at 2.2. The company agreed to stay for at least 10 years. (a) Calculate the total number of jobs created, including indirect and induced jobs, and the cost per job. (b) Evaluate the use of such incentives to attract manufacturing.
items.answer: (a) 1 760 jobs; US$51 136 per job (b) They bring jobs, skills and investment, but are costly per job, may attract footloose firms that leave when incentives end, and may simply move jobs from other regions.

items.stem: Table 8.2 shows scores (1 = poor, 5 = good) for three shoreline management policies at a stretch of eroding coast, with a weighting for each criterion. Protection of property (weight 3): hold the line 5, managed realignment 3, no active intervention 1. Cost (weight 2): hold the line 2, managed realignment 4, no active intervention 5. Environment (weight 2): hold the line 1, managed realignment 5, no active intervention 4. Effect on down-drift coasts (weight 2): hold the line 2, managed realignment 3, no active intervention 5. (a) Calculate the weighted total score for each policy. (b) Identify the policy that should be chosen on this evidence. (c) Explain why managed realignment may be preferred on coasts backed by farmland.
items.answer: (a) hold the line: 25; managed realignment: 33; no active intervention: 31 (b) Managed realignment (c) Low-value land does not justify the cost of defences; new salt marsh absorbs wave energy and creates habitat; it adapts to sea-level rise.

items.stem: A pastoral area in northern Burkina Faso covers 2 000 ha. Grass production averages 800 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 30% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. One tropical livestock unit (TLU) eats about 2 300 kg of dry matter a year. The present herd is 375 TLU. (a) Calculate the carrying capacity of the area in TLU. (b) Suggest why carrying capacity in a drought year would be lower. (c) Suggest how herders could manage the pasture more sustainably.
items.answer: (a) 209 TLU (b) Less rain means less grass growth, so the same herd exceeds the capacity; animals concentrate around remaining water. (c) Reduce herd size or sell animals before droughts; rotational grazing; move herds seasonally; fodder banks; water points spaced out; community grazing rules.

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a savanna grassland, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 27%, litter 8%, soil 65% of a total of 3 000 kg of nutrients per hectare. (a) Calculate the mass of nutrients in each store. (b) Calculate the ratio of the biomass store to the soil store. (c) Explain the relative size of the litter store. (d) Explain what would happen to the nutrient stores if the vegetation were cleared and burned.
items.answer: (a) biomass 810; litter 240; soil 1 950 kg/ha (b) 0.42 : 1 (c) Small in savanna because fire and termites remove litter quickly. (d) Biomass store removed (some nutrients released as ash, briefly enriching soil); with no canopy, heavy rain leaches and erodes the soil; the litter input stops; the cycle collapses.

items.stem: Corbel’s formula estimates limestone solution: X = 4ET ÷ 100, where X is the rate of solution (m³ per km² per year, equal to mm per 1000 years), E is annual runoff in decimetres and T is the mean concentration of dissolved CaCO₃ in mg/l. In the Burren, Ireland, E = 10 dm (1000 mm) and T = 79 mg/l. (a) Calculate the rate of solution. (b) Calculate how much the limestone surface would be lowered in 1 000 000 years at this rate. (c) Explain why solution rates in the humid tropics are usually higher than in temperate areas. (d) Suggest one limitation of Corbel’s formula.
items.answer: (a) 31.6 m³ per km² per year (31.6 mm per 1000 years) (b) 31.6 m (c) Higher runoff from heavy rainfall; high soil CO₂ from rapid decay of vegetation increases acidity; warm temperatures speed reactions. (d) It assumes all CaCO₃ comes from limestone in the basin and ignores solution underground, variation in runoff and concentration over time, and dolomite or other rocks.

items.stem: Table 9.1 classifies the 97 earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or more recorded in a period by tectonic setting: subduction (destructive) boundaries 70, collision boundaries 10, constructive boundaries 6, transform boundaries 8, intraplate locations 3. (a) Calculate the percentage of earthquakes in each setting. (b) Calculate the angle of the subduction-boundary sector if the data were shown as a pie chart. (c) Suggest why intraplate earthquakes can be very damaging even when infrequent.
items.answer: (a) subduction (destructive) boundaries 72.2%; collision boundaries 10.3%; constructive boundaries 6.2%; transform boundaries 8.2%; intraplate locations 3.1% (b) 260° (c) Buildings are not designed for earthquakes, people are unprepared, and old cold crust transmits shaking over large distances.

items.stem: “The supply of sediment is the most important factor in the formation of depositional coastal landforms.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to longshore drift and wave energy.
items.answer: For: Without sediment from cliffs, rivers and offshore, spits, bars and dunes cannot form; dams and defences that cut supply cause erosion (e.g. the Nile delta). Against: Wave energy and direction, longshore drift, coastal shape, tides, wind for dunes, vegetation and sea-level change also control formation. Conclusion: Sediment supply is a necessary condition, but the form and location of features depend on processes and coastal configuration.

items.stem: Assess the view that the movement of the ITCZ is the main factor explaining the climates of the tropics.
items.answer: For: The ITCZ brings convergence and convectional rain, controlling the timing and length of wet seasons from equatorial to savanna climates. Against: Subtropical highs, cold ocean currents, relief and rain shadows, monsoon pressure systems and ENSO also shape tropical climates; local factors create variation (e.g. the dry coast of Peru). Conclusion: The ITCZ is the main control over rainfall seasonality, but other circulation features and local factors are needed for a full explanation.

items.stem: Elena argues that aid does more to benefit donor countries than recipient countries. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to health and governance.
items.answer: For: Tied aid, political influence, access to markets and resources, contracts for donor firms; aid can create dependency. items.stem: To what extent do you agree that dependence on primary commodities is the main reason why some countries gain little from world trade? In your answer you may refer to tariffs and governance.
items.answer: For: Volatile and falling commodity prices, declining terms of trade, little value added (Zambia’s copper, Burundi’s coffee). Against: Tariff escalation, trade rules, lack of infrastructure, conflict, weak institutions and the power of TNCs also limit gains; some commodity exporters gain greatly (Botswana diamonds, Gulf oil). Conclusion: Commodity dependence is a key factor, but governance and the structure of trade rules determine whether countries benefit.

items.stem: Priya argues that the energy mix of a country is determined mainly by its physical resources. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to technology and resources.
items.answer: For: Resources shape the mix: Norway’s hydro, Kenya’s geothermal, South Africa’s coal, Saudi oil. Against: Wealth, technology, government policy (France’s nuclear programme after 1973, Germany’s Energiewende), climate commitments, prices and trade allow countries to import or develop alternatives. Conclusion: Physical resources give advantages, but policy, wealth and technology increasingly determine the energy mix.

items.stem: International tourists spent US$800 million in Kenya’s coast in one year. About 41% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 70% locally; each round of spending also leaks 41%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.7 × (1 − 0.41)). (a) Explain why leakage is high in many small tourist destinations. (b) Suggest how the destination could increase the multiplier effect.
items.answer: (a) Foreign-owned hotels and airlines send profits abroad; food, drink and building materials are imported; foreign managers; all-inclusive packages paid in the source country. (b) Encourage local ownership and suppliers (local food), train local staff for management jobs, limit all-inclusives, promote local crafts and excursions, tax foreign operators.

items.stem: A borehole on an atoll similar to Funafuti Atoll, Tuvalu passes through 1 222 m of shallow-water reef limestone before reaching volcanic basalt. The oldest reef limestone is about 50 million years old. Reef corals can grow upwards at about 5 mm per year. (a) Calculate how many times faster coral can grow than the island subsided. (b) Explain why the borehole evidence supports Darwin’s theory. (c) Explain why reefs have not always kept up with sea-level change.
items.answer: (a) about 205 times (b) Shallow-water corals cannot grow at depth, so their presence 1 km down shows the base has subsided while reef growth kept pace; the volcanic base confirms the original island. (c) Rapid post-glacial sea-level rise (up to 10-20 mm a year at times) and cooling or poor conditions slowed growth; some reefs drowned to form guyots.

items.stem: Table 21.1 shows the monthly mean PM2.5 concentration (µg/m³) in Lagos: Jan 84, Feb 63, Mar 45, Apr 35, May 27, Jun 25, Jul 16, Aug 15, Sep 22, Oct 52, Nov 84, Dec 84. The WHO annual guideline is 5 µg/m³ and the 24-hour guideline is 15 µg/m³. (a) Calculate the annual mean PM2.5 concentration and express it as a multiple of the WHO annual guideline. (b) State the number of months in which the monthly mean exceeded the 24-hour guideline. (c) Explain the effects of PM2.5 on human health. (d) Suggest how the city could reduce PM2.5 concentrations.
items.answer: (a) 46 µg/m³; 9.2 times the guideline (b) 11 months (c) Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing asthma, bronchitis, heart disease, stroke and lung cancer, and reducing life expectancy. (d) Cleaner vehicle fuels and emission standards; public transport and electric buses; closing or cleaning coal plants; controls on construction dust and waste burning; alternatives to stubble burning.

items.stem: Table 11.2 shows estimated peak winds (km/h), path length (km) and mean path width (m) of four tornadoes in Oklahoma: A: 163 km/h, 6.9 km, 50 m; B: 246 km/h, 28.9 km, 100 m; C: 114 km/h, 38.6 km, 200 m; D: 212 km/h, 32.9 km, 1200 m. EF scale (km/h): EF0 105-137; EF1 138-177; EF2 178-217; EF3 218-266; EF4 267-322; EF5 over 322. (a) Classify each tornado on the EF scale. (b) Calculate the area affected by each tornado (km²) and identify the largest. (c) Explain why a tornado with a lower EF rating may cause more deaths than one with a higher rating. (d) Explain the conditions that produce tornadoes in the Great Plains in spring.
items.answer: (a) A: EF1; B: EF3; C: EF0; D: EF2 (b) A: 0.34 km²; B: 2.89 km²; C: 7.72 km²; D: 39.48 km². Largest: D (c) It may cross a densely populated area, strike at night with little warning, or hit vulnerable buildings such as mobile homes, while a stronger tornado crosses open farmland. (d) Warm moist air from the Gulf of Mexico at low levels, dry air from the south-west above and cold air from the north create instability; the jet stream provides wind shear; supercells develop along the dry line and cold fronts.

items.stem: Briefly describe how agricultural change was managed, for India (Green Revolution in Punjab) or another example of the management of agricultural change in one country.
items.answer: India (Green Revolution in Punjab): From the mid-1960s: high-yielding wheat and rice, subsidised fertiliser and electricity for tube wells, minimum support prices and government procurement, agricultural universities and extension, credit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named policies, dates, actors and scale. [5]

items.stem: Fig. 17.3 shows mean wheat yields in India (tonnes per hectare): 1961: 0.85, 1970: 1.21, 1980: 1.44, 1990: 2.12, 2000: 2.78, 2010: 2.84, 2020: 3.43. (a) Identify the period with the largest increase and explain why yields rose rapidly then. (b) Suggest why yield growth slowed between 2000 and 2010. (c) Explain one environmental problem caused by the Green Revolution in Punjab.
items.answer: (a) 1980-1990 (+0.68 t/ha): spread of high-yielding varieties, expansion of tube-well irrigation, fertiliser subsidies and guaranteed minimum support prices. (b) Diminishing returns to fertiliser, soil degradation and falling water tables in Punjab, little new irrigated land, heat stress and limited new varieties. (c) Over-pumping of groundwater for irrigation has lowered water tables by about 0.5-1 m a year in places; or heavy fertiliser and pesticide use pollutes water and soils.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Corals obtain all their food by filter-feeding.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Compare fringing and barrier reefs.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Most food comes from the zooxanthellae. (b) Fringing reefs grow close to the shore with little or no lagoon; barrier reefs lie further offshore, separated by a wide, deep lagoon; barrier reefs are larger and often older.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Table 17.1 shows data for three farms: area (ha), number of workers and output (tonnes per hectare per year). wet rice farm, Bangladesh: 1.3 ha, 4 workers, 5.6 t/ha of rice; wheat farm, Saskatchewan, Canada: 830 ha, 3 workers, 3.2 t/ha of wheat; cattle ranch, Queensland, Australia: 44 366 ha, 4 workers, 0.0026 t/ha of beef (liveweight). Explain why the rice farm uses so much labour.
items.answer: Small plots, terracing, transplanting, weeding and water control are done by hand; labour is plentiful and cheap; capital for machinery is scarce.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the stages of the Butler model. (b) Explain the limitations of the Butler model.
items.answer: (a) Exploration (few adventurous visitors); involvement (local facilities); development (rapid growth, external investment); consolidation (growth slows); stagnation (capacity reached, reputation falls); then decline or rejuvenation. (b) Not all resorts follow every stage; timescales vary; difficult to identify the stage; ignores external shocks and planning; rejuvenation can happen repeatedly.

items.stem: Table 22.1 shows mean dissolved oxygen (mg/l) and the number of fish species recorded in the River Thames in London during a clean-up programme costing about €12 billion: 1985: 4.9 mg/l, 11 species; 1990: 6 mg/l, 16 species; 1995: 6.5 mg/l, 23 species; 2000: 7.4 mg/l, 30 species; 2005: 7.8 mg/l, 36 species; 2010: 8.9 mg/l, 44 species. items.answer: (a) species +300%; oxygen +81.6% (b) about €364 million per species

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Ghana (gold and cocoa): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 101, imports 106; 2019: exports 121, imports 112; 2021: exports 91, imports 121; 2023: exports 79, imports 125. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Explain what a falling terms of trade means for the country.
items.answer: It must export more to pay for the same quantity of imports, reducing real income, government revenue and the ability to repay debt.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the factors that increase the likelihood of slope failure. (b) A revision website states: “A longer storm can trigger landslides at a lower rainfall intensity.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Steep slopes; weak, weathered or jointed rock; bedding dipping parallel to the slope; saturation and high pore pressure; removal of vegetation; undercutting by rivers, waves or road cuts; loading by buildings; earthquake shaking. (b) Correct. Intensity-duration thresholds fall as duration increases.

items.stem: Fig. 14.3 shows discharge (m³/s) in a wash in Arizona, USA after a thunderstorm whose peak rainfall occurred at 0.5 hours: 0 h: 0, 1 h: 33, 2 h: 175, 3 h: 91, 4 h: 56, 5 h: 26, 6 h: 17, 8 h: 1, 10 h: 1. Before the storm the channel was dry. Suggest why flash floods are a hazard in desert towns.
items.answer: Little warning; people and roads in dry wadi beds; high sediment loads damage property; drivers underestimate depth (e.g. Jeddah 2009).

items.stem: Table 20.1 shows the approximate share (%) of electricity generation by source. Norway: hydro 88%, wind 10%, fossil fuels 2%. France: nuclear 65%, hydro 12%, wind and solar 13%, fossil fuels 10%. Norway generates about 250 TWh a year. (a) Suggest reasons for the energy mix of Norway. (b) Explain the problems of relying on one main source of electricity.
items.answer: (a) Mountainous relief, high rainfall and snowmelt and deep valleys give huge hydro potential; oil and gas are mostly exported. (b) Vulnerable to supply shocks (droughts reduce hydro, fuel price rises, plant outages); less energy security; may lock in high emissions.

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows mean track forecast errors (km) for Atlantic hurricanes at a forecasting centre. 1992: 24 h 190, 48 h 328, 72 h 512. 2023: 24 h 71, 48 h 120, 72 h 206. (a) Calculate the percentage change in forecast error at each lead time between 1992 and 2023. (b) Describe how forecast error changes with lead time in 2023. (c) Explain why reduced forecast errors save lives and money.
items.answer: (a) 24 h: −62.6%; 48 h: −63.4%; 72 h: −59.8% (b) Error increases with lead time, from 71 km at 24 h to 206 km at 72 h, about 2.9 times larger. (c) Warning areas can be smaller and more accurate, so evacuations are better targeted and trusted, fewer people are evacuated unnecessarily and more time is available to prepare.

items.stem: Table 18.2 shows the results of a fertiliser trial on rice in Punjab, India (nitrogen applied in kg/ha, yield in t/ha): 0 kg: 2.5 t, 50 kg: 4.6 t, 100 kg: 5.6 t, 150 kg: 6.1 t, 200 kg: 6.4 t, 250 kg: 6.5 t. (a) Calculate the increase in yield for each additional 50 kg/ha of nitrogen. (b) Explain the environmental impacts of applying fertiliser at high rates. (c) Suggest why farmers may apply more fertiliser than is economically worthwhile.
items.answer: (a) 0-50: 2.1 t; 50-100: 1 t; 100-150: 0.5 t; 150-200: 0.3 t; 200-250: 0.1 t (b) Unused nitrate leaches into groundwater and rivers, causing eutrophication and contaminating drinking water; nitrous oxide emissions; soil acidification. (c) Subsidised fertiliser prices; lack of soil testing and advice; insurance against poor soils; belief that more is better.

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 shows a weathering profile from a quarry in gneiss in Uganda. Thicknesses: soil and lateritic crust 2.1 m, completely weathered saprolite 19.7 m, partially weathered rock with corestones 8.6 m. The weathering front is below this. Dating suggests the profile developed over about 10 million years. (a) Calculate the depth of the weathering front below the surface. (b) Calculate the mean rate of advance of the weathering front in metres per million years. (c) Calculate the percentage of the profile made up of saprolite. (d) Explain the formation of corestones in the lower zone. (e) Suggest why the measured rate may be an underestimate of present-day weathering.
items.answer: (a) 30.4 m (b) 3.04 m per million years (c) 64.8% (d) Water penetrates along joints; hydrolysis attacks the edges and corners of joint-bounded blocks most rapidly, rounding them and leaving fresh cores surrounded by weathered material. (e) The top of the profile has been eroded; climate may have been drier in the past; dating is uncertain.

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows measurements of two waves recorded off the Holderness coast, England. Wave A: height 3.4 m, period 13 s. Wave B: height 1.4 m, period 10 s. Deep-water wavelength L = 1.56T² (metres, T in seconds). Waves with a steepness (H ÷ L) greater than 0.025 are usually destructive. (a) Calculate the deep-water wavelength of each wave. (b) Calculate the steepness of each wave and classify it as constructive or destructive. (c) Wave energy is proportional to H². Calculate how many times more energy wave A has than wave B. (d) Describe the effects of destructive waves on a beach profile. (e) Explain how wave refraction affects the distribution of wave energy along a coast of headlands and bays.
items.answer: (a) A: 263.6 m; B: 156 m (b) A: 0.013 (constructive); B: 0.009 (constructive) (c) 5.9 times (d) Plunging breakers with a strong backwash drag sediment offshore, forming offshore bars; the beach is lowered and a storm ridge may form at the top; the profile is flattened. (e) Waves slow in shallow water off headlands, bending so that orthogonals converge on the headland and diverge in bays; erosion is concentrated on headlands and deposition occurs in bays.

items.stem: Fig. 27.2 shows the share of the retail price (US$1200) of a smartphone captured at each stage of its global production network: brand owner (design, software, marketing) 45%, component makers (chips, screen, memory) 26%, retail and distribution 17%, final assembly 4%, other costs 8%. (a) Calculate the value captured at each stage. (b) Explain how a country could capture more value from the production network.

items.stem: Table 28.1 shows GDP per capita (thousand US$, PPP) by region in a country similar to Italy: North-west 25.7, North-east 19.8, Centre 19.6, South 18.2, Islands 15.3. (a) Calculate the ratio of the richest to the poorest region. (b) The standard deviation is 3.39. Calculate the mean and the coefficient of variation (CV = standard deviation ÷ mean × 100). (c) Suggest why the CV is a better measure of regional disparity than the ratio of richest to poorest. (d) Suggest limitations of using GDP per capita to measure regional disparities.
items.answer: (a) 1.68 (b) mean 19.72; CV 17.2% (c) It uses all regions rather than only the extremes and is independent of the units, allowing comparison between countries and over time. (d) It ignores inequality within regions, the cost of living, the informal economy and other aspects of well-being such as health and education.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Ghana (gold and cocoa): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 71, imports 102; 2019: exports 80, imports 115; 2021: exports 119, imports 110; 2023: exports 137, imports 109. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. (a) Calculate the terms of trade index for each year. (b) Explain what a falling terms of trade means for the country. (c) Suggest why the export price index fluctuated.
items.answer: (a) 2015: 100; 2017: 69.6; 2019: 69.6; 2021: 108.2; 2023: 125.7 (b) It must export more to pay for the same quantity of imports, reducing real income, government revenue and the ability to repay debt. (c) Commodity prices depend on world demand (Chinese growth), supply from other producers, weather and disease affecting harvests, speculation and exchange rates.

items.stem: Fig. 25.1 shows international tourist arrivals (millions): 1950: 25, 1980: 278, 1990: 435, 2000: 674, 2010: 952, 2019: 1465, 2020: 407, 2023: 1300. (a) Calculate the mean annual growth rate of arrivals between 1950 and 1990. (b) Calculate the percentage change in arrivals between 2019 and 2020. (c) Explain the growth in arrivals between 1950 and 2019. (d) Explain why arrivals fell in 2020 and recovered slowly.
items.answer: (a) 7.4% per year (b) −72.2% (c) Rising incomes and paid holidays, cheaper air travel, package and low-cost holidays, internet booking, growth of Asian middle classes and new destinations. (d) COVID-19 border closures, quarantine rules and flight cancellations; afterwards lost incomes, health fears, slow reopening in Asia and staff shortages.

items.stem: Table 18.2 shows the results of a fertiliser trial on wheat in Punjab, India (nitrogen applied in kg/ha, yield in t/ha): 0 kg: 2 t, 50 kg: 4.4 t, 100 kg: 5.5 t, 150 kg: 6.1 t, 200 kg: 6.4 t, 250 kg: 6.6 t. (a) Use the data to explain the idea of diminishing returns. (b) Explain the environmental impacts of applying fertiliser at high rates.
items.answer: (a) Each extra 50 kg adds less yield, falling from 2.4 t to 0.2 t, as other factors such as water, other nutrients and the crop’s genetic potential become limiting. (b) Unused nitrate leaches into groundwater and rivers, causing eutrophication and contaminating drinking water; nitrous oxide emissions; soil acidification.

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows the maximum sustained wind speed (km/h) of a tropical cyclone similar to Nargis (2008, Myanmar) on successive days: day 1 63, day 2 157, day 3 213, day 4 204, day 5 (after landfall) 88. Saffir-Simpson categories: 1: 119-153, 2: 154-177, 3: 178-208, 4: 209-251, 5: 252 or more. (a) Classify the storm on each day using the Saffir-Simpson scale. (b) Explain why the storm intensified over the first three days. (c) Explain why storm surge often causes more deaths than wind.
items.answer: (a) day 1: below hurricane strength; day 2: category 2; day 3: category 4; day 4: category 3; day 5 (after landfall): below hurricane strength (b) It moved over very warm ocean water (above 27 °C), with low wind shear; evaporation supplied moisture and condensation released latent heat, fuelling stronger winds. (c) Low pressure and strong onshore winds raise sea level several metres, flooding low-lying coasts and deltas quickly, e.g. Nargis in the Irrawaddy delta.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the formation of a spit. (b) Explain the formation of a tombolo.
items.answer: (a) Longshore drift carries sediment along the coast; where the coast changes direction, deposition continues out into the sea in sheltered, deeper water; wind and waves curve the end (recurved tip); a salt marsh forms behind. (b) Wave refraction around an island creates a zone of low energy behind it; longshore drift or swash-aligned deposition builds a ridge linking the island to the mainland.

items.stem: Country Q, an emerging economy, had GDP per capita (constant US$) of 1 500 in 2000 and 10 560 in 2025. Calculate the mean annual growth rate.
items.answer: 8.12% per year

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why governments try to manage energy supply. (b) Explain the challenges of an energy transition.
items.answer: (a) To ensure energy security, keep prices affordable, meet growing demand, reduce emissions to meet climate targets, reduce air pollution and widen access to electricity. (b) Intermittency and need for storage and grids; high investment costs; job losses in coal regions; public opposition to wind farms and pylons; energy prices; dependence on imports during transition.

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a tropical rainforest, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 78%, litter 4%, soil 18% of a total of 1 500 kg of nutrients per hectare. (a) Calculate the mass of nutrients in each store. (b) Calculate the ratio of the biomass store to the soil store.
items.answer: (a) biomass 1 170; litter 60; soil 270 kg/ha (b) 4.33 : 1

items.stem: In one year, a rainforest reserve in Costa Rica received 40 000 visitors. Each paid an entry fee of US$100 and spent an average of US$500 on accommodation, food and guides. About 45% of this spending leaked out of the local economy. Suggest how the reserve could prevent visitor numbers from damaging the ecosystem.
items.answer: Limit numbers by permit; zoning with trails; trained guides; boardwalks; seasonal closures; monitoring.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Ecotourism has no environmental impact.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Restricting visitor numbers always reduces income.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Flights and visitor activities still cause impacts. (b) Not correct. Higher-value visitors and fees can maintain or increase income.

items.stem: Table 18.1 shows the distribution of farm households and farmland by farm size in a region of Guatemala (% of households, % of land): under 1 ha: 52%, 4%; 1-5 ha: 28%, 11%; 5-20 ha: 12%, 22%; over 20 ha: 8%, 63%. Describe what the data show about land inequality.
items.answer: Highly unequal: 52% of households (under 1 ha) hold only 4% of land, while 8% (over 20 ha) hold 63%.

items.stem: Table 23.3 shows the share (%) of export earnings by product for Zambia in one year: copper 72%, cobalt 9%, maize and sugar 2%, tobacco 10%, other 7%. Total exports were US$45 billion, imports US$55 billion and GDP US$197 billion. (a) Explain the risks of such a high export concentration. (b) Suggest how the country could diversify its exports.
items.answer: (a) Earnings depend on the price and demand for copper; a fall in world prices or demand, or a supply shock, sharply reduces income, revenue and the ability to pay for imports. (b) Process raw materials domestically; develop other manufacturing and services; invest in infrastructure, education and SEZs; seek trade agreements; promote tourism and horticulture.

items.answer: (a) Country A: 51.6%; Country B: 96.7%; Country C: 87.5%; Country D: 85.7% (b) Debt is repaid in foreign currency, mainly earned from exports, so the ratio shows the share of foreign earnings used for repayments rather than imports or investment. items.stem: A grazing area in Darfur, Sudan covers 5 000 ha. Grass production averages 600 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 40% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. One tropical livestock unit (TLU) eats about 2 300 kg of dry matter a year. The present herd is 646 TLU. (a) Calculate the carrying capacity of the area in TLU. (b) Calculate the present stocking as a percentage of carrying capacity and state whether the area is overgrazed. (c) Suggest why carrying capacity in a drought year would be lower. (d) Suggest how herders could manage the pasture more sustainably.
items.answer: (a) 522 TLU (b) 123.8%: overgrazed (c) Less rain means less grass growth, so the same herd exceeds the capacity; animals concentrate around remaining water. (d) Reduce herd size or sell animals before droughts; rotational grazing; move herds seasonally; fodder banks; water points spaced out; community grazing rules.

items.stem: Table 11.2 shows estimated peak winds (km/h), path length (km) and mean path width (m) of four tornadoes in Oklahoma: A: 329 km/h, 31.4 km, 1200 m; B: 255 km/h, 10.5 km, 1200 m; C: 228 km/h, 12.8 km, 50 m; D: 172 km/h, 38.2 km, 200 m. EF scale (km/h): EF0 105-137; EF1 138-177; EF2 178-217; EF3 218-266; EF4 267-322; EF5 over 322. (a) Classify each tornado on the EF scale. items.answer: (a) A: EF5; B: EF3; C: EF3; D: EF1 (b) A: 37.68 km²; B: 12.6 km²; C: 0.64 km²; D: 7.64 km². Largest: A (c) It may cross a densely populated area, strike at night with little warning, or hit vulnerable buildings such as mobile homes, while a stronger tornado crosses open farmland. (d) Warm moist air from the Gulf of Mexico at low levels, dry air from the south-west above and cold air from the north create instability; the jet stream provides wind shear; supercells develop along the dry line and cold fronts.

items.stem: Name a case study of the management of a hazardous environment you have studied. For your example, evaluate the success of the management.
items.answer: Bangladesh (tropical cyclones): Deaths fell from about 300 000 (1970) to about 3400 (Sidr 2007) and 26 (Amphan 2020); but losses of homes, crops and land to salinity remain high, shelters can be overcrowded and poor women face barriers to evacuation.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that regional disparities are best reduced by investment in infrastructure. In your answer you may refer to governance, growth poles and education.
items.answer: For: Roads, railways, energy and broadband reduce isolation and costs (China’s western railways, EU-funded motorways); attract firms and tourism. Against: Infrastructure alone can increase backwash by making it easier to serve the periphery from the core; education, health, local enterprise, governance and cash transfers (Bolsa Família) may be more effective. Conclusion: Infrastructure is necessary but not sufficient; it must be combined with investment in people and institutions.

items.stem: Assess the view that wind is the most important agent in the formation of desert landforms. In your answer you may refer to weathering, dunes and past climates.

Against: Water, from rare floods and from wetter past climates, forms wadis, alluvial fans, pediments, playas and mesas and buttes; weathering prepares material. Conclusion: Wind is locally dominant, but water, past and present, is more important in shaping most desert landscapes.

items.answer: For: The poor depend directly on natural resources and may overuse land, forests and fuelwood; they lack capital for conservation. Conclusion: Poverty contributes locally, but wealth, consumption and industrial activity are the larger causes globally.

items.stem: Assess the view that the type of plate boundary is the main factor determining the hazards produced by tectonic activity.
items.answer: For: Boundary type controls magma type and eruption style, earthquake depth and magnitude (megathrust earthquakes and tsunamis at subduction zones). items.stem: Table 8.2 shows scores (1 = poor, 5 = good) for three shoreline management policies at a stretch of eroding coast, with a weighting for each criterion. Protection of property (weight 2): hold the line 5, managed realignment 2, no active intervention 1. Cost (weight 1): hold the line 2, managed realignment 3, no active intervention 5. Environment (weight 1): hold the line 1, managed realignment 4, no active intervention 5. Effect on down-drift coasts (weight 2): hold the line 2, managed realignment 3, no active intervention 5. (a) Calculate the weighted total score for each policy. (b) Identify the policy that should be chosen on this evidence. (c) Explain why managed realignment may be preferred on coasts backed by farmland.
items.answer: (a) hold the line: 17; managed realignment: 17; no active intervention: 22 (b) No active intervention (c) Low-value land does not justify the cost of defences; new salt marsh absorbs wave energy and creates habitat; it adapts to sea-level rise.

items.stem: Soil at a farm in the Nile delta, Egypt has an electrical conductivity (EC) of 10.1 dS/m. Relative yield (%) = 100 − b × (EC − a) when EC is greater than a, where a is the crop’s salinity threshold (dS/m) and b the % yield loss per dS/m above it. Values: rice: a = 3, b = 12; maize: a = 1.7, b = 12; tomato: a = 2.5, b = 9.9. (a) Calculate the expected relative yield of each crop. (b) State which crop the farmer should grow and why. (c) Explain how the soil may have become saline.
items.answer: (a) rice: 14.8%; maize: 0%; tomato: 24.8% (b) Tomato: it is the most salt-tolerant of the three, giving the highest relative yield. (c) Over-irrigation without drainage raised the water table; capillary rise and evaporation left salts at the surface; irrigation water added salts.

items.stem: Table 22.1 shows mean dissolved oxygen (mg/l) and the number of fish species recorded in the River Thames in London during a clean-up programme costing about €15 billion: 1985: 4.1 mg/l, 5 species; 1990: 5.2 mg/l, 10 species; 1995: 5.6 mg/l, 13 species; 2000: 6.6 mg/l, 20 species; 2005: 7.2 mg/l, 23 species; 2010: 8 mg/l, 33 species. (a) Calculate the cost of the programme per additional fish species recorded. (b) Explain why the number of fish species increased. (c) Suggest why the number of fish species is a limited measure of the success of the clean-up.
items.answer: (a) about €536 million per species (b) Better sewage treatment and controls on industrial discharges reduced organic pollution and toxins, so dissolved oxygen rose above the levels needed by sensitive species; fish passes and habitat restoration allowed recolonisation. (c) It ignores fish numbers, health and invertebrates; sampling effort may have increased; some species are introduced; contaminants in sediment may remain; other aims such as recreation and drinking water matter too.

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows measurements of two waves recorded off a beach in Cornwall, England. Wave A: height 2 m, period 11 s. Wave B: height 3.3 m, period 5 s. Deep-water wavelength L = 1.56T² (metres, T in seconds). Waves with a steepness (H ÷ L) greater than 0.025 are usually destructive. (a) Wave energy is proportional to H². Calculate how many times more energy wave A has than wave B. (b) Explain how wave refraction affects the distribution of wave energy along a coast of headlands and bays.
items.answer: (a) 0.37 times (b) Waves slow in shallow water off headlands, bending so that orthogonals converge on the headland and diverge in bays; erosion is concentrated on headlands and deposition occurs in bays.

items.stem: Corbel’s formula estimates limestone solution: X = 4ET ÷ 100, where X is the rate of solution (m³ per km² per year, equal to mm per 1000 years), E is annual runoff in decimetres and T is the mean concentration of dissolved CaCO₃ in mg/l. (c) Explain why solution rates in the humid tropics are usually higher than in temperate areas.
items.answer: (a) 25 m³ per km² per year (25 mm per 1000 years) (b) 2.5 m (c) Higher runoff from heavy rainfall; high soil CO₂ from rapid decay of vegetation increases acidity; warm temperatures speed reactions.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “China has become the largest source of international tourist spending.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “International arrivals recovered fully to 2019 levels in 2021.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Chinese outbound spending grew rapidly before 2020. (b) Not correct. Recovery took until about 2024.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the advantages of a mega-nourishment such as the Sand Engine. (b) Explain why the Holderness coast is difficult to manage sustainably.
items.answer: (a) One large placement disturbs the ecosystem less often than repeated nourishments; natural processes spread the sand along the coast; it creates recreational space and dunes; it adapts to sea-level rise. items.answer: (a) 35 m (b) A flat terrace of beach deposits backed by a relict cliff, sometimes with caves, arches and stacks now inland and vegetated.

items.stem: A coffee cooperative member in Peru sells 3 500 lb of coffee. The world market price is US$1.44 per lb. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$1.8 per lb (or the market price if higher), plus a Fairtrade premium of US$0.4 per lb. (a) Suggest how the cooperative could use the Fairtrade premium. (b) Explain why the benefits of Fairtrade may be limited.
items.answer: (a) Community projects such as schools, clinics and clean water; business investment such as processing equipment, organic conversion and training to improve quality. (b) Cooperatives can sell only part of their crop on Fairtrade terms; certification costs; hired labourers may not benefit; small share of the market; premium shared across members.

items.stem: Table 12.1 shows scores (1 = low, 10 = high) for hazard, vulnerability and capacity for four settlements on the slopes of a volcano: Settlement A: hazard 5, vulnerability 9, capacity 7; Settlement B: hazard 9, vulnerability 2, capacity 7; Settlement C: hazard 9, vulnerability 4, capacity 4; Settlement D: hazard 3, vulnerability 8, capacity 3. Risk = hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity. (a) Calculate the risk score for each settlement and rank them from highest to lowest risk. (b) Suggest two ways of increasing the capacity score of the highest-risk settlement. (c) Suggest limitations of using scores in the risk equation.

items.stem: Table 7.1 shows conditions at five sites in a tropical sea (water temperature °C, depth m, salinity ‰, water clarity): Site P: 28 °C, 50 m, 34‰, clear; Site Q: 33 °C, 5 m, 40‰, turbid; Site R: 31 °C, 20 m, 36‰, clear; Site S: 25 °C, 15 m, 35‰, turbid; Site T: 31 °C, 10 m, 34‰, clear. items.answer: (a) Site R and Site T (b) Site P: depth; Site Q: temperature, salinity, clarity; Site S: clarity (c) Coral grows in the shallow, sunlit water around the island; there has not been enough time for subsidence to form a lagoon and a barrier reef.

items.stem: Table 18.1 shows the distribution of farm households and farmland by farm size in a region of Guatemala (% of households, % of land): under 1 ha: 52%, 6%; 1-5 ha: 21%, 20%; 5-20 ha: 6%, 23%; over 20 ha: 21%, 51%. (a) Calculate the ratio of the share of land to the share of households for each farm size class. (b) Describe what the data show about land inequality. (c) Suggest the problems of land reform that redistributes land from the largest farms.
items.answer: (a) under 1 ha: 0.12; 1-5 ha: 0.95; 5-20 ha: 3.83; over 20 ha: 2.43 (b) Highly unequal: 52% of households (under 1 ha) hold only 6% of land, while 21% (over 20 ha) hold 51%. items.stem: Country Q, an emerging economy, had GDP per capita (constant US$) of 800 in 2000 and 2 520 in 2025. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in GDP per capita over the period. (b) Calculate the mean annual growth rate. (c) Use the rule of 70 to estimate how long it took GDP per capita to double. (d) Explain factors that may have contributed to this growth. (e) Suggest why GDP per capita growth may not reflect improvements for everyone.
items.answer: (a) +215% (b) 4.7% per year (c) about 14.9 years (d) Export-oriented manufacturing and FDI, investment in education and infrastructure, urbanisation moving workers into higher-productivity jobs, stable government policy, high savings. (e) Gains may go mainly to urban and coastal regions or the wealthy; inequality may rise; environmental costs; informal workers excluded.

items.stem: Table 9.1 classifies the 93 earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or more recorded in a period by tectonic setting: subduction (destructive) boundaries 60, collision boundaries 18, constructive boundaries 4, transform boundaries 7, intraplate locations 4. items.answer: (a) subduction (destructive) boundaries 64.5%; collision boundaries 19.4%; constructive boundaries 4.3%; transform boundaries 7.5%; intraplate locations 4.3% (b) Stress builds where the plates lock along a large, gently dipping fault (megathrust); the rupture area is very large, so the energy released is great; the Benioff zone extends deep.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the movement of the ITCZ is the main factor explaining the climates of the tropics. In your answer you may refer to ocean currents and the Hadley cell.
items.answer: For: The ITCZ brings convergence and convectional rain, controlling the timing and length of wet seasons from equatorial to savanna climates. items.answer: (a) +139 thousand m³ per year: a surplus, so beaches are likely to accrete. items.answer: (a) 6 of 10 pairs = 60% (b) Grants or low-interest loans for treatment plants; phased discharge limits; polluter-pays charges used for clean-up; negotiation through a river basin committee; publicising pollution data. items.stem: Fig. 2.1 shows a weathering profile from a borehole in granite in Nigeria. Thicknesses: soil and lateritic crust 3.3 m, completely weathered saprolite 17 m, partially weathered rock with corestones 4.8 m. The weathering front is below this. Dating suggests the profile developed over about 10 million years. (a) Calculate the mean rate of advance of the weathering front in metres per million years. (b) Explain the formation of corestones in the lower zone. (c) Suggest why the measured rate may be an underestimate of present-day weathering.
items.answer: (a) 2.51 m per million years (b) Water penetrates along joints; hydrolysis attacks the edges and corners of joint-bounded blocks most rapidly, rounding them and leaving fresh cores surrounded by weathered material. (c) The top of the profile has been eroded; climate may have been drier in the past; dating is uncertain.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why wadis have steep sides and flat floors. (b) Explain the formation of a playa.
items.answer: (a) Flash floods carry a large load and erode vertically and laterally; banks have little vegetation and collapse; sediment is spread across the floor as floods wane. items.answer: (a) 52 m³ per km² per year (52 mm per 1000 years) (b) 26 m (c) Higher runoff from heavy rainfall; high soil CO₂ from rapid decay of vegetation increases acidity; warm temperatures speed reactions. Level 3 (11-15): clear knowledge with appropriate examples; evaluation present but uneven or not fully supported. Level 2 (6-10): some knowledge, mainly descriptive; limited or general examples; little evaluation. Level 1 (1-5): basic, fragmented points; no examples. Level 0: no creditable response. Indicative content: Named policies, dates, actors and scale. A balanced judgement is required for Level 4.

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country A: 1970: 62%, 10%, 28%; 1990: 42%, 15%, 43%; 2010: 25%, 15%, 60%; 2025: 7%, 12%, 81%. (a) Calculate the change in the share of primary employment between 1970 and 2025, in percentage points and as a percentage change. (b) Describe how the changes fit the Clark-Fisher model.
items.answer: (a) −55 percentage points; −88.7% (b) Primary employment falls steadily; secondary rises with industrialisation and then falls; tertiary grows to become the largest sector, as the model predicts.

items.stem: A government gave a foreign car-parts company US$90 million in grants and tax relief to open a factory in an SEZ in India. The factory employs 2 000 people at an average wage of US$3 000 a year. The regional employment multiplier is estimated at 2. The company agreed to stay for at least 10 years. (a) Calculate the incentive cost per direct job. (b) Calculate the total number of jobs created, including indirect and induced jobs, and the cost per job. (c) Calculate the total wages paid to direct employees over 10 years. (d) Explain why the multiplier effect creates additional jobs.
items.answer: (a) US$45 000 (b) 4 000 jobs; US$22 500 per job (c) US$60 000 000 (d) The factory buys components and services from local suppliers, and employees spend wages in local shops, creating indirect and induced jobs; tax revenue funds services.

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 shows that the ITCZ migrates between about 5°S in January and 20°N in July over Africa. A student estimates that a station at 2°N lies within the rainy zone of the ITCZ for about 11 months of the year. (a) Suggest when the wet season occurs at this station. (b) Explain why places near the equator may have two rainfall maxima. (c) Explain why the dry season becomes longer with distance from the equator. (d) Suggest why the ITCZ moves further north over Africa and Asia than over the Atlantic Ocean.
items.answer: (a) two rainy seasons around the equinoxes (b) The ITCZ passes overhead twice a year, around the equinoxes, as it moves north and then south. (c) The ITCZ spends less time over places nearer its limits; for the rest of the year they are under the influence of the subtropical high and dry trade winds. (d) Land heats up more than the sea in summer, creating a stronger thermal low further from the equator.

items.stem: International tourists spent US$300 million in Jamaica in one year. About 21% of this spending leaked out of the economy immediately. Of the income that remains, local people re-spend about 56% locally; each round of spending also leaks 21%. The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.56 × (1 − 0.21)). (a) Calculate the multiplier and the total income generated in the local economy. (b) Explain why leakage is high in many small tourist destinations. (c) Suggest how the destination could increase the multiplier effect.
items.answer: (a) k = 1.79; total US$425 million (b) Foreign-owned hotels and airlines send profits abroad; food, drink and building materials are imported; foreign managers; all-inclusive packages paid in the source country. (c) Encourage local ownership and suppliers (local food), train local staff for management jobs, limit all-inclusives, promote local crafts and excursions, tax foreign operators.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Ghana (gold and cocoa): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 95, imports 103; 2019: exports 72, imports 113; 2021: exports 115, imports 121; 2023: exports 101, imports 112. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. (a) Calculate the terms of trade index for each year. (b) Suggest why the export price index fluctuated.
items.answer: (a) 2015: 100; 2017: 92.2; 2019: 63.7; 2021: 95; 2023: 90.2 (b) Commodity prices depend on world demand (Chinese growth), supply from other producers, weather and disease affecting harvests, speculation and exchange rates.

items.stem: Table 21.3 shows the estimated number of premature deaths attributed to air pollution in one year in four cities, with their populations: City A: 16 669 deaths, population 11.7 million; City B: 24 382 deaths, population 28.6 million; City C: 15 449 deaths, population 9.7 million; City D: 39 008 deaths, population 24.5 million. (a) Calculate the death rate per 100 000 people for each city. (b) Explain why rates are a better basis for comparison than total deaths. (c) Suggest why these estimates are uncertain.
items.answer: (a) City A: 142.5; City B: 85.3; City C: 159.3; City D: 159.2 (b) Cities have very different populations, so totals reflect size; rates show the risk to an individual. (c) Deaths are modelled from exposure-response relationships, not counted; monitoring stations are few; other causes of disease such as smoking overlap.
